title: Shorten Your Odds
hook: The strategy debate had been running for six weeks. Both sides had projections. Neither side had listed what would have to be true for their option to actually work.
counterintuition: The instinct under uncertainty is to gather more information until confidence arrives. The problem is that forward projection under genuine uncertainty produces more scenarios, not better decisions. The useful move is not to add more analysis but to reverse the direction: instead of projecting what might happen, ask what must be true for each option to succeed. That question produces a list of testable conditions, not a wider range of projections.
tryThisNow: For the strategic option you are most committed to right now, ask: what would have to be true for the one you are least convinced of to be the better choice? List three conditions. Check each one: evidence in hand, or assumption? The condition you cannot support is the first thing to investigate, not the last.
keyTakeaway: Shortening the odds under uncertainty means reverse engineering from a desired outcome to the specific conditions that must hold, then testing the most uncertain and most consequential conditions first rather than defending the most comfortable option.

breakdown.fastRead: Nils ran a restaurant and was weighing two options: a second location across town or a catering operation from his existing kitchen. The revenue projections looked good for both. When someone asked him to list what would have to be true for each option to succeed, the picture changed. For the catering path, he needed corporate clients at premium rates, a kitchen that could handle both service and catering without physical expansion, and a head chef willing to manage production scheduling. For the second location, he needed a neighborhood lunch crowd large enough to sustain a new spot, a manager who could run the existing location without him daily, and a landlord willing to negotiate the lease. Nils was not asking which option was safer. He was asking which assumptions each option was betting on that he could not yet verify. The catering path had two conditions he could test that week. The second location had three conditions he could not verify without signing a lease and committing a year of investment.
breakdown.deepRead:
The misunderstanding that blocks clear decisions under uncertainty is the belief that more analysis will eventually produce enough confidence to act. The problem is that forward projection under genuine uncertainty produces more scenarios, not better decisions. The output is a wider range of possibilities and the same unresolved disagreement about which option to choose.

The what-would-have-to-be-true approach works in the opposite direction. Instead of projecting forward from available data, it works backward from a desired outcome. For each strategic option under consideration, the question is: what must be true for this option to succeed? The answer is a list of conditions, not a single probability estimate. Some conditions can be verified now with existing data. Some require a small test before the full commitment. Some cannot be resolved without committing to the option and accepting the uncertainty. Instead of asking which option is right, ask what would have to be true for each option to work. The conditions that neither side can agree on are the ones worth testing before committing to either.

That is where to put the next week's effort.

The practical sequence is to list the conditions for each option, rank them by consequence, and identify which high-consequence conditions are currently supported only by assumption rather than evidence. A condition that is uncertain but low-consequence can wait. A condition that is certain but high-consequence is a known constraint, not a risk. The most dangerous condition is the one that is both most consequential and treated as assumed, not yet verified.
breakdown.fullRead:
Forward projection under uncertainty produces a useful feeling and a dangerous output. The feeling is rigor: multiple scenarios, probability estimates, sensitivity analyses. The output is a wider range of projections attached to the same unresolved strategic question. Adding another scenario does not resolve which option to choose; it extends the analysis phase and defers the commitment. The what-would-have-to-be-true approach changes the question being asked and, as a result, changes what the team does next.

The six examples above share a structural feature. In each case, the strategic debate was stuck because both sides were defending positions, not listing conditions. Sarah and her co-founder were arguing about which product path was safer. Matt's council was arguing about whether the repair estimate was credible. Julien's team was arguing about which market was larger. In each case, the stuck argument converted into a tractable question as soon as someone asked: what would have to be true for this option to work? The question produced a list. The list had items with different evidence quality. The items with the least support became the first tests.

A condition is useful when it is written specifically enough that a test can touch it. 'The market will respond well' is not a condition; it is a hope. 'At least twelve of thirty trial users will invite a teammate in week one' is a condition. 'The neighborhood will support a second location' is not testable. 'The block has at least eight hundred weekday lunch visitors who do not yet have a dedicated option' is a condition. The specificity requirement is not pedantic. It is what makes the condition honest, not merely reassuring.

Consider the option you are currently leaning toward on a decision you are carrying right now. What would have to be true for the option you are not leaning toward to actually be the better choice? Write the conditions for that option down. Now look at each condition and ask: do you have evidence for this, or are you assuming it? The conditions you are assuming but cannot yet verify are the ones your choice is actually resting on. If those conditions were false, would you still choose the same option? That is the question the analysis has not yet answered.

The uncertainty does not go away when you choose. But you can choose to test the most uncertain conditions before you commit, rather than discovering them after.

The order in which conditions are tested matters as much as the list itself. The temptation is to test the easiest condition first, because an easy test feels like progress and produces an early confirmation. But the easy condition is rarely the consequential one. The condition worth testing first is the one that, if false, would change the decision. A small pilot on the riskiest condition before the full commitment is more valuable than a large study on conditions that will not change the outcome.

Shortening the odds is not the same as eliminating uncertainty. A competitor can move after the commitment is made. A supplier can fail. Market behavior can shift in ways that no condition list predicted. The value of the what-would-have-to-be-true approach is not that it makes surprise impossible. It is that it converts avoidable ignorance into early tests. The surprises that remain are genuine surprises. The assumptions that were testable before the commitment are no longer acceptable as reasons for failure after it.

examples.title: Sarah Converts a Co-Founder Argument Into a List of Testable Conditions

planSpec.domain: an early-stage startup deciding between two product directions at a funding inflection point
planSpec.audience: two co-founders who disagree on whether to build a B2B tool or a B2C consumer app and are about to split the team over it
planSpec.stakes: the team will spend the next twelve months building one of these paths, and the other co-founder's buy-in depends on feeling like the choice was made on evidence, not politics
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sarah asks what would have to be true for the B2C path to win, and her co-founder lists conditions, not positions; the conversation converts from argument to testable propositions

examples.scenario: 'You keep saying B2B is safer,' Sarah's co-founder said. 'You haven't said what would have to be true for B2C to win.' Sarah paused. That was the question she had been avoiding. She wrote it at the top of the whiteboard: what must be true for B2C to work? Her co-founder started listing: high organic word-of-mouth so the acquisition cost stays low, conversion from free to paid that is faster than the category average, and a viral loop that works without influencer spending. Sarah wrote each condition down. Then she asked which of those conditions they could test in the next six weeks without committing to the full build. The argument stopped being about who was right. It became about which conditions were most uncertain and what the cheapest honest test looked like.
examples.whatToDo: When a strategic debate is stuck between two positions, stop arguing which option is correct and start listing what must be true for each option to succeed. Then identify which conditions are testable before full commitment and run those tests first.
examples.whyItMatters: Turning conditions into testable propositions changes the conversation from defending positions to investigating evidence. The co-founders were not disagreeing about facts; they were assuming different conditions. Making the assumptions explicit is the first step to resolving them.

examples.title: Matt Lists What Would Have to Be True Before the City Council Votes on the Bridge

planSpec.domain: a city infrastructure committee deciding between repairing an aging bridge and building a new crossing route
planSpec.audience: a public works director presenting a recommendation to a city council that is split between the repair and new-build options
planSpec.stakes: the repair option is cheaper and faster but rests on the assumption that the bridge can be made safe for twenty more years; the debate is stuck because neither side can prove their assumption without testing it
planSpec.requiredBeat: Matt presents the committee report and a council member asks what would have to be true for the repair option to be the right choice; the question converts the debate from cost comparison to condition verification

examples.scenario: At 2:15, Matt advanced to the slide comparing repair at four million and new build at twenty-two million. A council member in the third row raised her hand before he finished. 'Walk me through what would have to be true for the repair to be the right choice,' she said. Matt listed the conditions: the structural assessment must confirm twenty-year life, the foundation must be sound enough to hold the repaired load, and the contractor must be able to hold the budget through winter construction. The council member asked which of those three conditions they actually knew versus assumed. One was known. Two were assumed. The committee had a vote scheduled for Thursday and two conditions that had not yet been tested.
examples.whatToDo: Before bringing a cost comparison to a decision-maker, list the specific conditions each option requires and mark which are supported by evidence versus which are currently assumed. The assumed conditions on the lower-cost option are often the ones that determine whether the savings are real.
examples.whyItMatters: The council member's question converted a cost debate into a condition inventory. The two assumed conditions were the actual risk in the repair option, not the cost difference. Testing them before the vote was cheaper than discovering them during construction.

examples.title: Julien Discovers That Three Conditions Drive the Urban Launch Differently Than Assumed

planSpec.domain: a consumer product company evaluating two possible launch markets for a new product
planSpec.audience: a marketing director choosing between launching first in a large urban market and launching first in a smaller, more concentrated regional market
planSpec.stakes: the urban launch offers faster volume but requires a marketing budget the company does not have; the regional launch requires word-of-mouth growth that the company has evidence for from a similar product
planSpec.requiredBeat: Julien asks his team to list what would have to be true for each launch path to succeed and finds that the urban launch requires three conditions his company has never met, while the regional launch requires two conditions supported by existing evidence

examples.scenario: Which launch market was the right choice when the company could only afford one? Julien had predicted the urban market would win the argument on size alone. He asked his team to list what would have to be true for each path to succeed before the budget was allocated. The urban launch required a performance marketing budget the company did not have, a retail placement that would take six months to negotiate, and a customer acquisition cost below a threshold the company had never achieved in any market. The regional launch required word-of-mouth velocity that a similar product had demonstrated the previous year and a distribution partnership the company already had in that geography. The size argument had been true. The condition argument changed the decision.
examples.whatToDo: Before choosing between two launch paths based on market size, list the specific conditions each path requires and check which conditions have supporting evidence from prior experience. The path with better evidence quality on its load-bearing conditions is often the one worth trying first.
examples.whyItMatters: Market size is an outcome, not a condition. Julien's team had been debating which market was bigger when the real question was which conditions they already had evidence for. The condition list converted a size debate into an evidence inventory.

examples.title: Diego Finds the Single Most Uncertain Condition and Designs a Pilot Around It

planSpec.domain: a clinical research team evaluating two study designs for a new therapeutic approach
planSpec.audience: a research director choosing between a large randomized controlled trial and a smaller adaptive trial design
planSpec.stakes: the adaptive trial is faster and cheaper but depends on the assumption that early signals will be robust enough to adjust the protocol without introducing bias
planSpec.requiredBeat: before: Diego brings the two designs as a budget choice; after: he reframes each as a set of conditions and finds the single most uncertain condition for the adaptive trial is testable with a small pilot before either full design is committed

examples.scenario: Two study design proposals sat on the research committee table: the large randomized controlled trial on the left, labeled three years and full budget; the adaptive trial on the right, labeled eighteen months and sixty percent of the cost. Before: Diego framed the choice as a budget decision and the committee debated timelines. After: he asked what would have to be true for the adaptive trial to succeed and the conditions changed the conversation. The adaptive design required the early signal to be clean enough to adjust the protocol without introducing bias. That single condition was the most uncertain and the most consequential. It was also testable with a small preliminary study before either full design was committed. The committee stopped debating the budget and started planning the pilot.
examples.whatToDo: Before choosing between a faster, cheaper option and a slower, more expensive one, list the conditions for each and identify the single most uncertain condition on the faster option. If that condition is testable with a small pilot, run the pilot before committing to either full design.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost advantage of the adaptive trial was real only if the early signal condition held. That condition was testable before the commitment. Running a budget debate without first identifying the most uncertain condition meant the committee was evaluating the wrong question.

examples.title: Petra Shifts the Acquisitions Committee From Manuscript Evaluation to Condition Testing

planSpec.domain: an independent publisher choosing between two manuscript acquisitions with limited budget for one
planSpec.audience: a senior editor who must recommend one of two strong manuscripts to the acquisitions committee
planSpec.stakes: manuscript A is from an established author with a reliable audience; manuscript B is from a debut novelist whose early reader response was exceptional but untested at scale
planSpec.requiredBeat: Petra reviews previous debut acquisitions and reframes the question from which manuscript is better to what would have to be true for the debut to hit its target; she finds two of the three conditions are verifiable before the committee meeting

examples.scenario: Petra had reviewed the comparison document three times: prose quality, marketability, category fit, all rated for both manuscripts. The established author scored reliably. The debut scored exceptionally on prose and unevenly on everything else. She put the comparison document aside and asked a different question: what would have to be true for the debut to reach its target? The conditions were specific. The exceptional reader response must hold across a broader test group, not just the original early readers. The social media following must represent genuine engagement, not inflated counts. The category must have room for a new voice in the current season. Petra could verify two of the three before the committee meeting. She brought the condition list instead of the comparison document.
examples.whatToDo: Before making an acquisition decision based on evaluation criteria, ask what conditions must hold for the riskier option to succeed. Identify which conditions are verifiable before the commitment and gather that evidence before the decision meeting.
examples.whyItMatters: The comparison document ranked both manuscripts on the same criteria and could not resolve the debate. The condition list gave the committee something actionable: two conditions worth verifying before committing the budget to either manuscript.

examples.title: Frida Prepares for the Investment Committee's Question About Site B's Conditions

planSpec.domain: a real estate development team evaluating two sites for a mixed-use project
planSpec.audience: a development director whose team has built strong business cases for both sites but whose investment committee needs a clearer basis for choice
planSpec.stakes: site A has established foot traffic but higher land cost; site B has lower land cost but uncertain demand growth in a transitional neighborhood; both cases look good on paper but depend on different assumptions
planSpec.requiredBeat: Frida imagines presenting both sites to the investment committee and being asked what would have to be true for Site B to be the right choice; the question converts the pro forma debate into a condition inventory with clear next tests

examples.scenario: You are preparing both site presentations for the investment committee and you already know the question that will come. Site B's pro forma is strong, but the committee will ask: what would have to be true for this site to be the right choice? Frida ran through the conditions before the meeting. Neighborhood demand growth must continue at its current pace through the three-year construction period. The zoning approval must proceed on the projected timeline without the variance that would add a year. The anchor tenant must commit before construction begins, not after. The pro forma assumed all three. The first condition was supported by two years of demand data. The second was assumed. The third was the condition that had sunk three previous transitional-neighborhood projects in the region. She knew which condition to test before the committee meeting and what the test would cost.
examples.whatToDo: Before presenting a business case to an investment committee, anticipate the 'what would have to be true' question for the riskier option and prepare condition-specific answers. Identify which conditions are assumed versus supported and have a plan for the most uncertain one.
examples.whyItMatters: The pro forma comparison made both sites look attractive. The condition inventory showed that Site B's advantage rested on three assumptions, one of which had a documented history of causing project failures. That condition, not the pro forma, was the real decision variable.

questions.prompt: Why does the 'what would have to be true' question help teams make better decisions under uncertainty?
choices: To identify which strategic option has the most supporting data before the decision is made
To determine which team members have the most confidence in each strategic option
To convert forward projections into a list of specific conditions that each option requires in order to succeed
questions.explanation: The question reverses the direction of analysis: instead of projecting forward from available data, it works backward from a desired outcome to the conditions that must hold. The output is a list of conditions, not a confidence ranking.

questions.prompt: Two co-founders are arguing about whether to build a B2B or B2C product. Sarah asks: 'What would have to be true for the B2C path to win?' Her co-founder lists three conditions. What should the team do next?
choices: Analyze the market size for each option to determine which has more revenue potential
Identify which conditions are testable in the next six weeks without committing to the full build, and run those tests first
Survey potential customers to determine which product type they would prefer before making the decision
questions.explanation: Once conditions are listed, the next step is to sort them by testability before full commitment. The conditions that can be tested cheaply before the major investment are the ones that should be tested first. Market size analysis and customer surveys are useful but do not test the specific conditions that could change the decision.

questions.prompt: Matt presented a bridge repair option at four million dollars versus a new build at twenty-two million. A council member asked what would have to be true for the repair to be the right choice. Matt identified three conditions: one supported by evidence and two assumed. What does this reveal?
choices: The cost comparison was the wrong frame; the two assumed conditions are the actual risk in the repair option and should be tested before the vote
The repair option is likely to cost more than projected because assumed conditions often lead to budget overruns
The council should delay the vote until the contractor can provide a binding cost guarantee for all three conditions
questions.explanation: The assumed conditions are where the cost advantage of the repair option can fail. Testing them before the vote is cheaper than discovering them during construction. The cost comparison gave the council a false sense of which decision was lower risk.

questions.prompt: Julien's team found that the urban launch required three conditions his company had never met, while the regional launch required two conditions supported by existing evidence. Which action follows from this finding?
choices: Commission a new study on whether the urban market conditions could be met before making a final decision
Split the launch budget between both markets to test the conditions for both simultaneously
Choose the regional launch path because it has better evidence quality on its load-bearing conditions
questions.explanation: The condition inventory showed that the regional launch had supporting evidence for its key conditions while the urban launch required capabilities the company had never demonstrated. That evidence quality difference, not market size, is the strategically relevant finding. The regional path has better-supported conditions.

questions.prompt: Diego's research committee was debating between an eighteen-month adaptive trial and a three-year randomized controlled trial. After listing the conditions each design required, the committee found the single most uncertain condition for the adaptive trial was testable with a small preliminary study. What is the correct next step?
choices: Run the preliminary study to test the most uncertain condition before committing to either full design
Proceed with the randomized controlled trial because it has fewer uncertain conditions
Request additional budget to fund both designs simultaneously so the committee can evaluate the results in parallel
questions.explanation: When the most uncertain condition for the riskier option is testable before full commitment, the correct step is to run that test. The preliminary study provides evidence on the condition that determines whether the faster path is viable, at a fraction of the cost of committing to either full design.

questions.prompt: Petra reframed the manuscript acquisition debate from 'which manuscript is better' to 'what would have to be true for the debut to hit its target.' She found two of the three required conditions were verifiable before the committee meeting. What principle does this illustrate?
choices: Evaluation criteria are not useful for acquisition decisions because they cannot capture the conditions that drive commercial success
Reframing a comparative evaluation as a condition inventory reveals which conditions are testable before the commitment and gives the decision a concrete next step
The established author is always the safer choice because debut novels have more untested conditions than experienced authors
questions.explanation: The comparison document could not resolve the debate because it ranked both manuscripts on criteria that did not reveal the specific conditions driving the risk. The condition list gave the committee something actionable: evidence to gather before the meeting, not subjective ratings to debate.

questions.prompt: Frida identified that Site B's pro forma rested on three conditions: two supported by data and one with a documented history of causing project failures in similar neighborhoods. What is the most strategically sound way to present this to the investment committee?
choices: Recommend Site A because the presence of any high-risk assumed condition makes Site B's pro forma unreliable regardless of the other conditions
Present the condition inventory with the evidence quality for each condition and a specific plan for testing the most uncertain one before committing to Site B
Present both pro formas with sensitivity analysis showing the committee what happens if each condition fails
questions.explanation: The condition inventory gives the committee the actual information driving the decision: which conditions are supported and which are assumed. The plan to test the most uncertain condition before committing shows the committee a path to reduce the risk before committing, not simply accept or reject the site. Recommending Site A on the basis of one uncertain condition ignores the possibility that the condition is testable. Sensitivity analysis shows what happens if conditions fail but does not reduce the uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A planning team has been asked to choose between two options. The team has extensive analysis on both but keeps returning to the same disagreement. Which action most directly applies the 'what would have to be true' approach?
choices: Commission additional market research to resolve the disagreement with more data
Escalate the decision to senior leadership who can resolve the impasse with a final call
Ask each side to list the conditions their option requires, then identify which are assumed rather than supported by evidence
questions.explanation: When analysis has not resolved a strategic disagreement, the problem is usually that both sides are defending positions, not examining conditions. Asking each side to list specific conditions converts the debate into an evidence inventory and identifies the assumptions that are actually driving the disagreement.

questions.prompt: Why is the order in which conditions are tested strategically important?
choices: The condition that is both most consequential and most uncertain should be tested first, because a failed test on that condition is the one that should change the decision
Testing easier conditions first builds team confidence and momentum before addressing the harder ones
Conditions should be tested in the order they were identified to maintain a consistent process
questions.explanation: Testing easy conditions first produces early confirmation but avoids the assumption that most threatens the decision. The condition worth testing first is the one that, if false, would change the choice. Easy tests on low-consequence conditions do not improve the odds; they generate activity that avoids the real question.

reviewCards.front: What does the 'what would have to be true' question produce that forward projection does not?
reviewCards.back: A list of specific conditions that each option requires in order to succeed, rather than a wider range of projections. The conditions can be ranked by consequence and evidence quality, which the projections cannot.

reviewCards.front: How do you sort a condition list once you have written it?
reviewCards.back: Rank by consequence (if this condition is false, how much does it matter?) and by current evidence quality (supported by data, or assumed?). The conditions that are most consequential and least supported by evidence are the ones to test first.

reviewCards.front: What makes a condition testable rather than vague?
reviewCards.back: A testable condition is written specifically enough that a test can touch it. 'The market will respond well' is not testable. 'At least twelve of thirty trial users will invite a teammate in week one' is testable. The specificity is what makes the test honest.

reviewCards.front: When a strategic debate is stuck between two positions, what does the 'what would have to be true' question change?
reviewCards.back: It converts the debate from defending positions to listing conditions. The conditions that both sides disagree about are the assumptions driving the disagreement, not the facts. Making the assumptions explicit is the first step to resolving them through evidence.

reviewCards.front: Does the 'what would have to be true' approach eliminate uncertainty?
reviewCards.back: No. Competitors can move, suppliers can fail, and behavior can shift after the commitment. The value is that it converts avoidable ignorance into early tests. The surprises that remain after testing the most uncertain conditions are genuine surprises, not assumptions that could have been checked.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to reverse engineer from a desired strategic outcome to the specific conditions that must hold, then rank those conditions by consequence and evidence quality so the most uncertain and most consequential ones get tested before the full commitment is made.

ifThenPlans.context: when a strategic debate is stuck between two options and more analysis is not resolving it
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask each side to list what must be true for their preferred option to succeed. The conditions that both sides disagree about are the assumptions driving the disagreement. Run a test on the most uncertain one before continuing the debate.

ifThenPlans.context: when preparing a recommendation for a decision-maker
ifThenPlans.plan: Before finalizing the recommendation, list the conditions the preferred option requires and mark which are supported by evidence versus assumed. Present both the recommendation and the condition inventory so the decision-maker can see what has and has not been verified.

ifThenPlans.context: when a team is about to commit budget to a strategic option
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask what would have to be true for the option that is not being chosen to be the better decision. List the conditions for that option and check the evidence quality. The conditions you cannot support are the ones to investigate before the budget is committed.

ifThenPlans.context: when facing a decision with significant uncertainty
ifThenPlans.plan: Write the conditions for each option. Identify the single most uncertain condition for the option that appears most attractive. Ask what it would cost to test that condition before the full commitment. If the test is cheaper than the cost of being wrong, run it first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take a decision you are currently carrying and write the conditions for each option: what must be true for each one to succeed. Mark each condition as either supported by evidence or currently assumed. Name the one assumed condition that would most change your thinking if it turned out to be false. That is the first thing to investigate.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, each time you hear a strategic debate stuck on positions, ask what would have to be true for each side to be correct. Write the conditions for both positions. At the end of the week, review which conditions were testable and which were not. The testable conditions that nobody tested are the places where the team could have shortened its odds.

memorableLines.text: Nils was not asking which option was safer. He was asking which assumptions each option was betting on that he could not yet verify.
memorableLines.why: The reframe from 'safer' to 'which assumptions cannot yet be verified' captures the precise move the approach makes: it shifts the question from comfort to testability.

memorableLines.text: Instead of asking which option is right, ask what would have to be true for each option to work. The conditions that neither side can agree on are the ones worth testing before committing to either.
memorableLines.why: This two-sentence formulation gives the reader the exact question to ask and the exact output to look for. It is the practical instruction compressed into two sentences.

memorableLines.text: The uncertainty does not go away when you choose. But you can choose to test the most uncertain conditions before you commit, rather than discovering them after.
memorableLines.why: The two-sentence contrast acknowledges that uncertainty is real while giving the reader an action that is genuinely within their control. It closes the argument without false reassurance.
